prose.title: C-Town Chivalry Cleared the Decks in July and Bought McCaffrey and Burrow at the Auction
prose.dek: Bear Dunn has the best roster in the league: no holes and {{f.team.0009.studs_today}} studs. He finished it at the auction, after releasing two expensive players in July and watching other owners pay almost the same money for them weeks later.

paragraphs: The backfield ranks {{f.team.0009.rb_rank}}, first in the league, and it is not an argument. Christian McCaffrey grades High-end RB1. James Cook also grades High-end RB1. Breece Hall, a Mid RB2, fills a flex. No other backfield starts two backs graded High-end RB1 or better.
Jaxon Smith-Njigba is an Elite WR1 carrying a league-minimum salary this season. Tee Higgins is a Mid WR2 and Tetairoa McMillan another in the flex, and the room ranks {{f.team.0009.wr_rank|ord}}.

Brock Bowers grades Elite TE1, though a knee injury has him listed doubtful and expected to miss the opener, and tight end ranks {{f.team.0009.te_rank|ord}}. Joe Burrow is a High-end QB1 with Jayden Daniels at Mid QB1 in the superflex, ranking {{f.team.0009.qb_rank|ord}}. None of the priced offensive slots is a hole, and {{f.team.0009.holes_today}} holes is the joint-best figure in the league.

The defense came cheap. Five of seven defensive starters grade replacement-level, only Budda Baker at Mid DB2 and Xavier McKinney at Low-end DB2 rate at all, and every one of them but McKinney came from the Free Agent Auction at the league minimum or a whisker above it.

In April he had {{f.team.0009.active_roster_opening}} active players carrying {{f.team.0009.cap_opening}} in salary, and the quality was already there: {{f.team.0009.studs_opening}} top-twelve players among the priced positions and just {{f.team.0009.holes_opening}} hole, where the best player he had to fill it was Tony Pollard, a Replacement-level RB.

Between April and the auction lock he went backwards, down to {{f.team.0009.active_roster_preauction}} active players carrying {{f.team.0009.cap_preauction}} in salary. Drake London left in a three-way trade that brought back Tetairoa McMillan, which left Tee Higgins as his second receiver. Pollard was released the day the roster locked, and the hole simply moved: the best quarterback he had left for the superflex was Tua Tagovailoa, a Replacement-level QB.

The auction fixed it. He came out with {{f.team.0009.active_roster_current}} active players, {{f.team.0009.studs_postauction}} studs, {{f.team.0009.holes_postauction}} holes and a starting offense that gained more at the auction than anyone else's. Christian McCaffrey took the first back slot and pushed James Cook to the second, which pushed Breece Hall into a flex, which pushed McMillan into the other one. Joe Burrow took quarterback and moved Jayden Daniels into the superflex, where the last hole had been. Six of the nine priced slots got a new occupant, and he finished with the strongest starting offense in the league.
One buy at the Expired Rookie Auction — Brian Branch for {{f.team.0009.era_spend}}, out of a pool of {{f.league.era_pool_size}} players whose rookie deals ran out without earning a second one.

At the Free Agent Auction he won {{f.team.0009.faa_lots_won}} players for {{f.team.0009.faa_spend}}, and the shape of it is stark. Christian McCaffrey cost {{f.team.0009.top_buy_price}}, {{f.team.0009.top_buy_pct_of_spend}} of the total, and drew more bids than any other player in the auction. Joe Burrow cost nearly as much again. Those two players took the overwhelming majority of his budget.

Measured against the money, only Blake Bombers shopped better. He spent {{f.team.0009.faa_off_spend}} on offense at the Free Agent Auction, and for what that money bought he ranks {{f.team.0009.faa_off_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}. Blake Bombers spent less and got more for each dollar; CBP improved almost exactly as much but paid more to do it, Real Deal Creel spent more than anybody for less, and C-Town did it from a lineup that already had its studs in place, with less room to improve than most.

McCaffrey is worth pausing on. Sex Manther had tagged him in May and released him in July, at which point he became the most contested player of the summer and landed here for a price barely above what that tag had been. One owner tagged him to keep him, let him go without a penalty two months later, and handed the league's best roster its first-choice running back.

Everything else was volume: DK Metcalf aside, the rest are a wall of minimum or near-minimum buys, most of them uncontested, Cooper Kupp among them. That wall is also six of his seven defensive starters, and defenders took {{f.team.0009.idp_auction_spend}} in all, {{f.team.0009.idp_auction_share}} of his auction money.

captions.t.0009.faa_value: Ranked by how much each owner's starting offense improved between the auction lock and the close, for every dollar he spent on quarterbacks, backs, receivers and tight ends at the Free Agent Auction.

paragraphs: {{f.team.0009.contracts_count}} contract moves, {{f.team.0009.trades_count}} trade, {{f.team.0009.roster_removals_total}} removals. The removals are where the cleverness lives.

On the day the auction roster locked he released George Pickens, one of the largest salaries on his books, and took no penalty at all — the entire amount came straight back to him. Tony Pollard went the same day at a smaller salary, this one carrying a penalty. Within two weeks L.A. Looks had bought Pickens at auction for close to what C-Town had been paying him, and CBP had bought Pollard for slightly more than C-Town had been paying him.

He turned two contracts he no longer wanted into cap room just before the auction, and two rival owners then spent real auction budget acquiring them. That room went toward McCaffrey and Burrow. Pickens had arrived after April, so his release handed back money he had taken on during the offseason; Pollard's release, penalty and all, is the one that freed salary he had carried since April.

The bill is not zero. {{f.team.0009.cuts_penalty_unstamped}} of penalty from his releases has no charge year stamped on it yet, so it sits in the ledger unassigned. Nothing has hit this season at {{f.team.0009.cuts_penalty_2026}}, but that figure is real and it will land somewhere.

Sam LaPorta was extended in May and now sits on the bench as a Mid TE1 behind an Elite TE1, which is a lot of salary for a backup. James Cook was extended and restructured the same day, and the restructure cut his current-year charge sharply. Burrow was signed to a two-year back-loaded deal. The rest turned five defensive auction buys into multi-year deals, three of them at the league minimum and two just above it.

The one trade is the three-way with Real Deal Creel and Blake Bombers. He sent Drake London and {{f.team.0009.trade_blind_bid_cash}} of blind-bid money to Blake Bombers and received Tetairoa McMillan from Real Deal Creel. London is the better receiver, so he gave up more than he got back and paid cash on top of it, and his was the only side of the deal to send out both talent and money. Three-way trades are rare in this league, and this is the only one completed through the league's trade tool.
The rookie class barely exists: {{f.team.0009.rookie_picks_count}} picks, both defenders, both late, neither priceable by any source yet. He was not drafting this year.

He is {{f.team.0009.division_rank|ord}} of {{f.team.0009.division_size}} in his division, ahead of Cleon Ca$h and the Hawks, and he plays each of them five times. Cleon Ca$h is a genuine threat, but the Hawks are last in the league, and five games a year against the softest opponent available is a real structural advantage on top of everything else.

Is this the strongest team in the league? Yes. {{f.team.0009.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}, {{f.team.0009.holes_today}} holes, {{f.team.0009.studs_today}} studs, the strongest starting offense anybody has, and first at running back. Was it a good offseason? Also yes, and the two answers are connected rather than coincidental — he spent {{f.team.0009.auction_spend}}, and part of the room for it came from releasing Tony Pollard and George Pickens on the day the roster locked, just before the market for both of them opened.

The biggest advantage is the offense top to bottom, with an Elite WR1 on a league-minimum salary this season as the keystone. The biggest weakness is the bill: {{f.team.0009.cuts_penalty_unstamped}} of release penalty still has no charge year, and if it lands on this season it is more than the {{f.team.0009.cap_current_room}} of room he has now. The thin defense matters less; it is the cheapest problem in the league to fix.

{{f.league.wk_teams_final}} NFL teams had played when this was written, and Jaxon Smith-Njigba caught a long touchdown among eight receptions and banked {{f.team.0009.wk_points_final}} points. That was the highest score by any player in the league that night.
